      Your sample contains

      The blueprint for the whole plant. The DNA in the nucleoplasm holds the instructions for every root, stem, leaf and flower.

      Nearly every cell in the plant carries a complete copy.

      Vacuole — Osmosis & Turgor Lab

      OSMOSIS
      MEASURED
      SpecimenPlant cell, central vacuole
      DeliveredATP (MIT-08), vesicle (GOL-06)
      Water gatesAquaporins in the plasma membrane and tonoplast
      RuleWater moves toward higher solute concentration
      Fig. 11 — Live osmosis benchTurgid
      Outside is—
      Ψs outside—
      Ψs vacuole—
      Ψp turgor—
      Net water flow—
      Vacuole volume—
      Trial log
      #OutsideVacuoleΨpVolumeCell state
      No trials yet. Set the sliders, let the cell settle, then press Record trial. Try all three solutions.
      Three kinds of solution
      Outside solutionCompared with the vacuoleNet water movementPlant cell becomes
      HypotonicFewer solutes outsideInto the cell and vacuoleTurgid: the vacuole swells and presses on the wall. The healthy state for a plant.
      IsotonicEqual solutesNo net movement (equal in and out)Flaccid: soft, no turgor; the plant starts to wilt
      HypertonicMore solutes outsideOut of the vacuole and cellPlasmolyzed: the membrane pulls away from the wall
      Water potential (Ψ) — how the readouts are calculated
      TermMeaningFormula / sign
      ΨWater potential: water flows from higher (less negative) Ψ to lower ΨΨ = Ψs + Ψp
      ΨsSolute potential: dissolved solutes lower itΨs = −CRT (0 for pure water, negative otherwise)
      ΨpPressure potential: the wall pushing back on a swollen protoplast (turgor)0 or positive

      Why plants need a wall: in fresh water an animal cell can swell until it bursts, but a plant cell's wall pushes back, so it becomes firm instead; that turgor holds up leaves and stems. In the field: wilting is loss of turgor, and salty soil or over-applied fertilizer makes the soil solution hypertonic, pulling water out of roots (fertilizer burn). Values are calculated with C in osmoles per liter at 20 °C (RT ≈ 2.44 L·MPa/mol); the model is simplified for teaching.

      Stages of cellular respiration (per glucose)
      StageWhereInputsOutputsATP
      GlycolysisCytosol, outside the mitochondrionGlucose (2 ATP invested)2 pyruvate, 2 NADH2 net
      Pyruvate oxidationMatrix2 pyruvate2 acetyl-CoA, 2 CO₂, 2 NADH0
      Krebs (citric acid) cycleMatrix2 acetyl-CoA (2 turns)4 CO₂, 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂2

      Mitochondrion anatomy
      PartRole
      Outer membraneSmooth outer boundary; lets small molecules in
      Intermembrane spaceH⁺ ions are pumped in here and build up
      Inner membraneHolds the electron transport chain and ATP synthase
      CristaeFolds of the inner membrane that add surface area
      MatrixFluid where pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle run; has its own DNA and ribosomes
      ATP synthaseA rotor turned by H⁺ flowing back into the matrix; each turn makes ATP

      The electricity: electrons from NADH and FADH₂ flow down the electron transport chain like a current. Their energy pumps H⁺ ions across the inner membrane, and the ions rushing back through ATP synthase spin it like a turbine. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor, which is why it becomes water. ATP yield is approximate: about 30–32 per glucose by current estimates (older textbooks say 36–38). Plants too: plant cells respire day and night, and respiration is the reverse of the photosynthesis equation in Sample CHL-07. Some flowers, such as skunk cabbage, use a plant-only alternative oxidase in their mitochondria to release energy as heat and warm themselves.

      Why leaves look green: chlorophylls absorb strongly in blue and red light and poorly in green (Fig. 8, approximate curves), so green light is reflected. Rubisco, the enzyme that fixes CO₂ in the Calvin cycle, is often called the most abundant protein on Earth. The Calvin cycle's direct product is G3P, a 3-carbon sugar; two G3P make one glucose, which the plant uses for energy or links into starch and cellulose. Next stop: carry your glucose to the mitochondrion.

      Processing log

      Cis faceToward the ERVesicles from the ER fuse here. Enzymes (mannosidases) trim extra mannose sugars off the sugar tag.
      MedialMiddle of the stackNew sugars are added: GlcNAc caps on the branches.

      Plant Golgi: a plant cell has many separate Golgi stacks that glide along actin filaments. Besides finishing proteins, they build cell-wall polysaccharides such as pectin and hemicellulose; cellulose itself is made at the plasma membrane. Many scientists think the cisternae themselves mature from cis to trans, carrying their cargo along; the figure shows the cargo's path through the stack. Next stop: your vesicle waits in the backpack until you reach the vacuole.

      Endoplasmic Reticulum — Protein Processing

      QUALITY
      CHECK PASSED
      SpecimenPlant cell, rough ER lumen
      InputProtein chain from Sample RIB-04
      HelpersSignal peptidase, BiP, PDI, calnexin

      Fig. 5 — Processing in the ERThreading
      Processing log
      StepHelperWhat happens
      ThreadingTranslocon (Sec61 channel)A signal peptide at the start of the chain docks the ribosome on the ER, and the chain is fed through a channel into the lumen as it is made.
      Signal peptide cutSignal peptidaseThe signal peptide has done its job and is snipped off.
      Sugar tagOligosaccharyl­transferaseA branched sugar chain is attached to an asparagine (N) as it enters: N-linked glycosylation.
      FoldingBiP chaperoneChaperones hold the chain so it folds into its working 3D shape instead of clumping.
      Disulfide bondPDITwo cysteines (C) are linked by an S–S bond that locks the fold in place.
      Quality controlCalnexinThe protein is checked. Misfolded proteins are held back or destroyed; good ones are released.
      ExportCOPII vesicle coatA patch of ER membrane buds off around the protein, forming a transport vesicle bound for the Golgi.
      Rough ER vs. smooth ER
      RegionSurfaceMain jobs
      Rough ERStudded with ribosomesMakes, folds and checks proteins for membranes, the vacuole and export from the cell
      Smooth ERNo ribosomesMakes lipids such as membrane phospholipids and oils; stores calcium ions

      In a real cell this happens while the ribosome is still translating: the ribosome sits on the ER and feeds the chain straight in. The chain in Fig. 5 is drawn longer than your 7-amino-acid fragment so the folding can be seen. Next stop: the vesicle carries the protein to the Golgi body.

      Analytical Report · Sample RIB-04

      Ribosome — Translation Assay

      PROTEIN
      SYNTHESIZED
      SpecimenPlant cell ribosome (80S)
      TemplatemRNA from Sample NUC-02
      AdapterstRNAs, anticodon ↔ codon
      Product7-amino-acid polypeptide
      Fig. 4 — Translation in progressInitiation
      Polypeptide (N-terminus → C-terminus)
      A site—
      Amino acids0 / 7
      Codon → anticodon → amino acid
      #Codon (5′→3′)Anticodon (3′→5′)Amino acid
      Stages of translation
      StageWhat happens
      InitiationThe small subunit binds the mRNA and finds the AUG start codon. The initiator tRNA carrying methionine pairs with it in the P site, then the large subunit joins.
      ElongationA tRNA whose anticodon matches the codon in the A site docks. The ribosome joins the growing chain onto its amino acid (a peptide bond), then shifts one codon along the mRNA. The empty tRNA leaves from the E site.
      TerminationA stop codon reaches the A site. No tRNA matches it; a release factor binds instead, the chain is let go, and the subunits separate.

      E · P · A sites: exit, peptidyl (holds the growing chain) and aminoacyl (receives the next tRNA). Next stop: the new chain is still floppy; on the rough ER it is threaded inside to be folded into its working shape. This 7-amino-acid chain is an illustrative fragment; real plant proteins are usually hundreds of amino acids long.

      Stages of transcription
      StageWhat happens
      InitiationRNA polymerase binds the gene's promoter and unzips a short stretch of DNA, opening a transcription bubble.
      ElongationThe polymerase reads the template strand and links matching RNA nucleotides into a growing mRNA strand.
      TerminationAt the end of the gene the polymerase lets go, the DNA zips back up, and the new RNA is released.

      Next stop: before it leaves, the new RNA gets a protective cap, has its non-coding pieces (introns) spliced out, and gains a poly-A tail. Then it exits through a nuclear pore to a ribosome. The 8-codon sequence shown is an illustrative teaching fragment, starting with the AUG start codon and ending with a UAA stop codon.

      Mission Briefing

      Field Researcher: Plant Cell Lab

      Your role

      You are a cell biology researcher who has been shrunk down to microscopic size. Your assignment: slip into a living plant cell, find each structure, and collect samples for the lab.

      Along the way you will follow the cell's own production line: copy a gene, build a protein, fold and package it, then make the sugar and energy the cell runs on.

      Moving around

      • Rotate: click and drag (one finger on a touchscreen).
      • Zoom: scroll the mouse wheel (pinch on a touchscreen).
      • Reset Orbit brings the view back to the start.

      Exploring on your own

      • Follow the orange glow: click the glowing structure in the Cell Structures list to read what it does. The glow then moves to the next one.
      • You can also click structures right on the cell. A ✓ marks each one you have explored.
      • When all 14 are explored, Start Guided Tour lights up.

      Guided tour

      • Press Start Guided Tour. Each stop asks a question in the sidebar; click the structure that answers it.
      • A wrong click gives you a hint.
      • At the first stop, the structure glows orange when you find it; click it again to go in. After that, each stop opens by itself when you are right.
      • Any button you need to press next glows orange.

      Collecting samples

      • Inside each stop, press the dashed button to collect your sample or item.
      • A lab report opens. Scroll through it, then leave to reach the next stop.
      • Your Backpack holds everything you collect; some items get delivered to later stops.
      • Text hard to read? Press Magnify at the top of any stop, then move over the words to see them larger. While it is on, the button turns orange and reads Lens off; press it (or Esc) to put the lens away.

      Lab tools (bottom bar)

      • Auto-Rotate: slowly spins the cell.
      • Fluorescence: boosts the colors, like a fluorescence microscope.
      • Z-Section: slices the cell from the top; drag the slider to cut deeper.

      Your field report

      When your backpack is full, press Export field report in the sidebar, type your name, and download a one-page PDF to turn in.
